editorNote: The home-computer boom is becoming a contest over what people can do together: play, bargain, program, and communicate.
morningLine: This week, four joysticks turn an Atari into a noisy frontier marketplace while a wave of new machines crowds the fall starting line.

lead.headline: M.U.L.E. Turns the Atari Into a Four-Player Marketplace
lead.dek: Ozark Softscape and Electronic Arts mix land development, arcade action, and a live commodity auction into one unusually social computer game.
body: A new game from designer Dani Bunten and Ozark Softscape asks Atari owners to gather around one machine and build an economy together. M.U.L.E., published by Electronic Arts, supports as many as four players, with the computer taking any empty places, and makes unusually direct use of the Atari computer family's four controller ports.

Each colonist claims plots on the planet Irata and outfits mechanical M.U.L.E.s to produce food, energy, smithore, or the riskier crystite. The choices interlock: energy keeps production moving, food buys time, and smithore supplies new machines. A player who ignores the colony's needs can discover that private advantage is hard to sustain.

The market is the game's great piece of theater. Buyers and sellers move their figures toward one another in a real-time auction, testing prices while everyone watches. Between rounds, short arcade sequences and random events keep the balance unsettled, so arithmetic never entirely replaces reflexes or nerve.

Computer Gaming World's July-August issue gave the title feature treatment beside Suspended and Battle for Normandy. In a season crowded with new hardware, M.U.L.E. makes the strongest case that the home computer's future may depend as much on inventive shared software as on another memory specification.

stories.headline: Seventeen New Computers Crowd the Fall Starting Line
stories.dek: Coleco's bundled Adam and a showroom full of rivals intensify the fight for the family desk.
body: COMPUT! counted at least 17 personal computers introduced at the Summer Consumer Electronics Show in Chicago and predicted that 30 to 40 sub-$1,000 machines could confront Christmas shoppers. The range ran from minimal 2K machines near $40 to elaborate systems above $1,000, a display of abundance that also warned how little room remained for undistinguished newcomers.

Coleco supplied the sharpest retail proposition. Its promised sub-$600 Adam combined an 80K Z80A computer, detachable keyboard, high-speed 500K-per-cassette drive, daisy-wheel printer, word processor, Microsoft BASIC, controllers, and Buck Rogers Planet of Zoom. A $450 add-on was promised for ColecoVision owners.

The bundle shifts the argument from the price of a keyboard to the cost of a usable system. Printers, storage, software, and a familiar game all arrive in the box—on paper, at least—putting pressure on rivals whose low advertised prices require a shopping list of accessories.

stories.headline: Atari Sweeps Away Its Old Line for Four XL Computers
stories.dek: The 400, 800, and short-lived 1200XL give way to a new ladder beginning at $199.
body: Atari has completely restructured its home-computer line, replacing the 400, 800, and recently introduced 1200XL with four XL models. The 16K 600XL carries a suggested $199 price, while the 64K 800XL is marked at $299; both include BASIC and full-stroke keyboards while retaining broad compatibility with older Atari software and peripherals.

Higher up, the proposed 1400XL adds a direct-connect 300-baud modem and speech synthesis. The 1450XLD adds a built-in double-sided, double-density disk drive storing as much as 254K. Together the machines are Atari's answer to a price war that has made yesterday's range look expensive almost overnight.

Atari Publishing is also preparing software for Commodore and Texas Instruments machines, a striking acknowledgment that software can travel where hardware sales do not. The reset preserves the familiar Atari graphics and sound strengths while admitting that the company must compete at several price points at once.

stories.headline: C and Scientific Software Reach the Personal-Computer Desk
stories.dek: An exact-week science column and BYTE's C-language issue point beyond the household budget program.
body: The New York Times devoted its August 2 Personal Computers column to new software for science and engineering, evidence that specialized calculation and analysis packages are becoming a recognizable microcomputer category. The personal machine is being asked to serve laboratories and technical offices, not merely play games or balance a checkbook.

BYTE's August theme issue, The C Language, follows the same movement toward more ambitious work. Its coverage of compilers, portability, and applications brings a language associated with institutional Unix systems before a broad microcomputer audience.

C cannot erase the incompatibilities among Apple, Atari, CP/M, and IBM machines, but portable source code offers programmers a way to think beyond a single box. That promise matters greatly in a week when the hardware showroom seems to acquire another incompatible family every few steps.

worldAnchor.headline: Thomas Sankara Takes Power in Upper Volta
